title: Survivorship bias
objectives: Condition on survival and see how it inflates the average fund return
Rebuild the full average from survivors and failures
Spot survivorship in backtests and track records

screens.prose: A database lists the equity funds that launched ten years ago and are still open today. Their average return has been 7% a year.

state.caption: Average of the seven: 7% a year

screens.question: Is 7% a year a fair estimate of the average return of all funds that launched ten years ago?

options.text: Fair: it averages every fund in the database
options.why: The database holds only funds still open. Funds that did badly may have closed and dropped out.
Funds that close are more often the losers. Leaving them out pushes the average up, not down.

hints.text: Which funds launched ten years ago but are not in the database?
A fund that closed is no longer listed.
Funds tend to close after poor returns, so the missing funds are mostly losers.

feedback.correct: The database only shows the funds that survived.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the funds that launched but are no longer listed.

explain.text: Only funds still open are listed. Funds usually close after poor returns, so the missing funds drag the true average down. The next screen shows all ten that launched.

screens.prose: Here are all ten funds that launched ten years ago, with their returns up to today or to the day they closed.
screens.question: Tap every fund with a negative return.

hints.text: A negative return has a minus sign.
Three funds lost money.
Funds 3, 6 and 9 have negative returns.

feedback.correct: The three losers are exactly the three funds that closed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only the rows with a minus sign in the return column.

byKey.low: Fund 8 returned 4% a year: low, but positive. Tap only the negative returns.
byKey.r7: Fund 8 returned 4% a year, which is positive.

explain.text: You tapped Funds 3, 6 and 9, and every one of them has closed. Closure was not random: it picked out the losers. So a database of open funds shows the winners only.

screens.prose: Today’s database keeps only the open funds, so we condition on survival.
screens.question: What is the average return of the open funds, in % a year? This is $E[R \mid \text{survived}]$.

hints.text: Add the returns of the seven open funds.
The open funds are the rows still at full strength.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the seven open funds’ returns and divide by 7.

byKey.all: That is the average of all ten funds. Here we want only the seven still open.
byKey.over-ten: You divided the survivors’ total, 49, by 10. Only seven funds are open, so divide by 7.

explain.text: The seven open funds add up to 49, so $E[R \mid \text{survived}] = 7$% a year. That is what the database shows. Now we put the closed funds back.

screens.prose: Now put the three closed funds back in. They lost 12%, 8% and 5% a year before closing.
screens.question: What is the average return of all ten funds, in % a year? This is $E[R]$.

widget.label: Average return of all ten funds

hints.text: Add all ten returns, including the negative ones.
The closed funds add up to −25.

feedback.correct: All ten funds averaged 2.4% a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the ten returns, negatives included, then divide by 10.

byKey.surv: That is the survivors’ average again. Put the three closed funds back in.
byKey.dropped: You divided by 10 but left out the closed funds’ losses. Add −12, −8 and −5 to the total.
byKey.sign: You added the losses as gains. The closed funds returned −12, −8 and −5.

explain.text: All ten add up to $49 - 25 = 24$, so $E[R] = 2.4$% a year. The survivors’ 7% overstates it by 4.6 points. Measuring only what survived is **survivorship bias**.

screens.prose: Split the ten funds by what happened to them: 7 survived and 3 closed.
screens.question: What is the average return of the closed funds, $E[R \mid \text{closed}]$, in % a year?

hints.text: Add the three closed funds’ returns.
−25 over 3 funds.

feedback.correct: The closed funds averaged about −8.33% a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the three closed funds only.

byKey.pos: The closed funds lost money. Keep the minus sign.
byKey.ten: You divided −25 by all ten funds. Divide by the three that closed.

explain.text: $E[R \mid \text{closed}] = -\tfrac{25}{3} \approx -8.33$. Weighting the two groups by their shares rebuilds the whole: $0.7 \times 7 + 0.3 \times (-8.33) = 2.4$. That is total probability, applied to averages.

screens.prose: Edge case. Suppose instead three of the ten funds closed because their managers retired. Which three was pure chance, unrelated to returns.
screens.question: On average, how does the survivors’ average compare with the 2.4% of all ten?

options.text: About the same: no bias on average

options.why: That needs closures to pick out the losers. Random closures remove good and bad funds alike.
Random closures are as likely to remove a winner as a loser. Nothing pushes the average down.

hints.text: Does a random closure prefer good funds or bad ones?
Each fund is equally likely to close.
If closure is independent of returns, $E[R \mid \text{survived}] = E[R]$.

feedback.correct: Random closures leave the survivors’ average unbiased.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the closures favour any kind of fund.

explain.text: If closure is independent of returns, survival tells you nothing about $R$, so $E[R \mid \text{survived}] = E[R] = 2.4$% on average. Any one sample can still miss by luck. The bias comes from closure that depends on returns, not from closure itself.

screens.prose: A fund family’s brochure makes a claim. “Every one of our funds has beaten the 3% cash rate over ten years.” It lists only the seven open funds.
screens.question: What share of the ten funds that launched beat 3% a year? Give a percentage.

widget.label: Share of funds that beat cash

hints.text: Count the funds above 3% among all ten.
None of the closed funds beat cash.
All 7 open funds beat 3%; none of the 3 closed funds did. 7 of 10.

feedback.correct: 7 of the 10 funds beat cash, not all of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use all ten funds as the bottom of the fraction.

byKey.survivors: You used the surviving funds as the sample: 7 of 7. The brochure dropped the three closed funds, none of which beat cash.
byKey.three: That is the share that did not beat cash. The question asks for the share that did.

explain.text: All seven open funds beat 3%, so $P(\text{beat cash} \mid \text{survived}) = 1$. But across all ten launches it is $\tfrac{7}{10}$. The brochure is true and misleading: it conditions on survival without saying so.

screens.prose: Why do survivors overstate? Let $S$ be survival and $R$ a fund’s return. Show how far $E[R \mid S]$ sits from $E[R]$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $E[R] = P(S)\,E[R \mid S] + P(S^c)\,E[R \mid S^c]$: split all funds into survivors and closed funds
$E[R] - E[R \mid S] = P(S^c)\big(E[R \mid S^c] - E[R \mid S]\big)$: subtract $E[R \mid S]$, using $P(S) = 1 - P(S^c)$
So survivors overstate whenever closed funds did worse, and not at all when $E[R \mid S^c] = E[R \mid S]$

hints.text: Start by splitting the whole into survivors and closed funds.
The gap line comes from subtracting $E[R \mid S]$ from the split.
Split, subtract, put in the numbers, then read off when the gap is zero.

feedback.correct: The bias is the closure rate times how much worse the closed funds did.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the split of all funds into two groups.

byKey.sub: The subtraction works on the split, so the split comes first.
byKey.nums: The numbers go into the gap formula, so that line comes after it.

explain.text: The gap is $P(S^c)$ times the difference between closed and surviving funds. Here that is $0.3 \times (-15.33) = -4.6$ points. If closure is unrelated to returns the difference is zero, and so is the bias.

screens.prose: You backtest buying the index from ten years ago. Of its 100 stocks then, 80 are still in it (they returned 9% a year) and 20 were dropped after falling (−6% a year). Today’s members include 20 newcomers that rose into the index (20% a year).
screens.question: An honest backtest buys the stocks in the index ten years ago. What average return does it give, in % a year?

widget.label: Average return of the original members

hints.text: Which stocks could you have bought ten years ago?
Ten years ago you held the 80 stayers and the 20 that were dropped.

feedback.correct: The original members returned 6% a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the 100 stocks that were in the index ten years ago.

byKey.today: That is today’s members: the 80 stayers plus the 20 newcomers. Ten years ago you could not know which stocks would join. That is look-ahead through survivorship.
byKey.stayers: You dropped the 20 stocks that fell out of the index. You would have held them too.
byKey.all: You averaged all 120 stocks. The newcomers were not in the index ten years ago.

explain.text: The original 100 returned $0.8 \times 9 + 0.2 \times (-6) = 6$% a year. A backtest on today’s members gives $0.8 \times 9 + 0.2 \times 20 = 11.2$%, nearly double. Using today’s constituents is look-ahead: it uses survival information you could not have had.

screens.prose: A quant team reports that its 5 live strategies returned 8% a year on average. In the same period it tried 15 others that lost 3% a year on average and were quietly abandoned.
screens.question: What was the average return of all 20 strategies the team tried, in % a year?

widget.label: Average return of all strategies tried

hints.text: Weight each group by how many strategies it holds.
15 of the 20 strategies were abandoned.

feedback.correct: The team’s ideas lost a quarter of a per cent a year on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the returns of all 20 strategies, then divide by 20.

byKey.reported: That is the reported average, conditioned on being kept. The abandoned 15 are part of the record too.
byKey.plain: You averaged 8 and −3 equally. Three times as many strategies were abandoned.
byKey.sign: You added the abandoned strategies’ losses as gains. They returned −3% a year.

explain.text: All 20 strategies averaged $\tfrac{40 - 45}{20} = -0.25$% a year. The reported 8% conditions on survival. Ask for the count of everything tried before you trust a track record.

ideas: Averaging only what survived gives $E[R \mid \text{survived}]$, not $E[R]$.
When failure depends on the outcome, survivors overstate. The bias is the failure rate times how much worse the failures did.
If failure is unrelated to the outcome, the survivors are a fair sample.

formula.name: Survivorship gap
formula.tex: E[R] - E[R \mid S] = P(S^c)\big(E[R \mid S^c] - E[R \mid S]\big)
formula.note: Zero when closure does not depend on returns.

summary.trap: Using the surviving universe as the sample, as a fund database or today’s index does.

quiz.prose: In the Second World War, analysts mapped bullet holes on bombers that returned. Most holes were on the wings and fuselage; few were on the engines.
quiz.question: Where should extra armour go?

options.text: On the wings and fuselage, where the holes are
options.why: You studied only planes that came back. Planes hit in the engines mostly did not return, so their holes are missing.
The pattern is informative once you ask which planes are missing from it.

feedback.correct: The missing planes were hit where the survivors were not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which planes are missing from the sample.

explain.text: The sample is conditioned on returning home. Few engine hits among survivors means engine hits rarely let a plane survive. So armour goes where the survivors show no holes.

quiz.prose: A hedge fund index includes the 60 funds alive today, which averaged 9% a year. Another 40 funds started at the same time and died, averaging −3% a year.
quiz.question: What was the average return of all 100 funds, in % a year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the two groups by their shares of the 100.

byKey.alive: That is the survivors’ average. Put the 40 dead funds back.
byKey.plain: You averaged 9 and −3 equally. The groups hold 60 and 40 funds.

explain.text: $0.6 \times 9 + 0.4 \times (-3) = 5.4 - 1.2 = 4.2$% a year. The index of live funds overstates by 4.8 points.

quiz.prose: A data vendor drops 30% of funds from its records at random, because of a storage fault. The dropped funds’ returns played no part.
quiz.question: Is the average return of the funds left biased?

options.text: No: on average it matches the average of all funds
Yes, upwards, as with any missing funds
options.why: Missing funds bias the average only when what goes missing depends on returns. A random fault does not.
A random fault drops good and bad funds alike.

feedback.correct: Random loss leaves the average unbiased, though noisier.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the loss depends on returns.

explain.text: The loss is independent of returns, so $E[R \mid \text{kept}] = E[R]$. The sample is smaller and noisier, but it is not biased.

quiz.prose: A book studies 50 billionaire founders and finds that most left university early. It concludes that leaving university helps you succeed.
quiz.question: What is the main flaw?

options.text: It looks only at successes; people who left and failed are not in the sample

options.why: A bigger sample of billionaires has the same flaw. The failures are still missing.

options.text: There is no flaw: most of them did leave
options.why: That is true of the survivors. It says nothing about the chance of success for people who leave.

feedback.correct: The sample is conditioned on success.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who is missing from the sample.

explain.text: The book measures $P(\text{left early} \mid \text{success})$. The claim needs $P(\text{success} \mid \text{left early})$, which requires the many who left and did not succeed.
